passage:
I'm Shreya, and last September I was the girl who swore she'd start physics revision "properly" in October. Every evening at seven, Nazia sent the same message: "One match? Just one."
The board exam was in March, which felt like a different planet. The match was right there, loud and bright, with my team waiting. One match became four. My physics notebook sat under the charger.
I told myself a few evenings couldn't change a grade in March. Looking back, what gets me is how sharp the game felt and how blurry March felt, even though March was the thing I actually cared about. In January I counted: sixty evenings, gone. After that, the controller went into Ammi's cupboard until nine.

qa.q: Where did Shreya's physics notebook sit while she played?
qa.a: The physics notebook sat under the charger.

qa.q: Why did 'just one match' feel reasonable to Shreya each evening?
qa.a: The match was loud, bright and happening now, while the March exam felt like a different planet, so one evening seemed too small to matter.

qa.q: Which choice finally helped Shreya, and why could it work?
qa.a: Putting the controller in Ammi's cupboard until nine meant she no longer had to win the fight with herself every evening; the study hour came first by default.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel if Shreya starts saying no to the seven o'clock match?
qa.a: Nazia might miss their evening game or feel a bit let down at first, but could also be pushed to think about the same exam.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing a nightly game over revision because the exam months away feels faint compared with the fun right now.

Mentor note: Tejas, Class 10, 14 November
Tejas came to the after-school study room today, sat down with his maths sheet, and within ten minutes was watching a friend's game on his phone under the desk. When I asked, he said, "The prelims are in February, ma'am. One round now won't matter."
He isn't careless. He told me he really wants the science seat next year. But the seat feels far off, and the game is happening right now.
We agreed on one change: his phone stays in my tray for the first forty minutes, and he has written the prelim date and the seat he wants on a sticky note on his desk. If he finishes the sheet, he gets the phone back for fifteen minutes of play.
Vinita, class mentor

qa.q: What did Tejas say when Vinita asked about the phone?
qa.a: He said, "The prelims are in February, ma'am. One round now won't matter."

qa.q: Why does 'one round' seem harmless to Tejas even though he wants the science seat?
qa.a: The seat is months away and feels vague, while the game is vivid and happening now, so a single round looks too small to cost anything.

qa.q: Why might the phone tray and the sticky note help Tejas?
qa.a: The tray removes the pull of the game for forty minutes, the note keeps the goal in view, and the fifteen minutes of play give him a reward he can feel today.

qa.q: How does Vinita view Tejas, and why does that matter for him?
qa.a: Vinita sees him as someone who wants the seat, not a careless student, so Tejas gets a practical plan instead of a lecture and is more likely to try it.

passage:
After school in the small town of Rahuri, the cyber café behind the bus stand was the only place with fast internet. Devika, fifteen, went there every day at four to play a racing game with the boys from Class 10.
Her friend Manjula found her there on a Wednesday in November. "The science practical file is due in March, and Sir said the board marks count for college."
"March," Devika said, eyes on the screen. "That's four months. This is the final lap."
"You said that last week."
"I'll do the whole file over Diwali."
Manjula sat on the plastic stool beside her and waited. The race ended. Devika bought another half hour with her bus money and said she'd walk home.
Manjula walked with her, carrying both their bags, the empty practical file sticking out of Devika's.

qa.q: What did Devika buy with her bus money?
qa.a: Another half hour at the cyber café.

qa.q: Why does Devika keep choosing the game over the practical file?
qa.a: The final lap is exciting and happening now, while March and college marks feel four months away and not quite real, so the game keeps winning.

qa.q: What choice could Devika make on the next Wednesday to help herself?
qa.a: She could do one page of the practical file with Manjula before going to the café, and let the game be the reward afterwards.

qa.q: What is the walk home like for Manjula?
qa.a: Manjula carries both bags and sees the empty practical file, likely feeling worried for Devika and unsure how to get through to her.

grounding: It shows a teenager preferring gaming now over better marks months later, because distant benefits feel weak and the game feels vivid.

Monday. Hansa's chemistry unit test was two weeks away. "Tonight, one hour of revision," she promised her brother Asif. Then his new racing game came out, and she took the second controller. "One race." It was midnight when she looked up.
The next Thursday. Still no revision. Every evening the game glowed, bright and fun, and the test felt like something that belonged to a different Hansa, in a different week.
The Monday after. The test paper had four questions on equilibrium. She knew one. Walking out, she could already see the marks, and for the first time the test felt more real than the game. At home she asked Asif to change the console password until Friday.

passage: Shreya, I see you with that phone game every night, and it reminds me of my Class 10. I, Rashmi, your very serious bua, spent that winter at the video game parlour near the bus stand in Ludhiana. One rupee a game. Every evening I told myself: the boards are in March, that's far away, tonight just one game. By January the high score on the fighting game was mine. My maths book was still in its plastic cover. Then my friend Harpreet came to the parlour one evening, not to play, but holding her mock-test result: sixty-two. Mine was thirty-nine. I sat on the parlour steps and cried. That night I gave my tokens to my younger cousin, and I studied every evening at Harpreet's house till March. I passed. Just.

passage: Zainab got exactly one free hour a day, from nine to ten, after closing up her father's tailoring shop in Bhopal. The science olympiad was in April, four months away, and Himani had lent her last year's papers. Every night at nine she meant to open them. Every night her thumb opened the farming game instead: the crops were ready, the cows needed feeding, a little chime rewarded every tap. April felt like another planet. By December the papers were still clipped together under her pillow. When Himani messaged, "Done paper 3? It's hard!!", Zainab felt a hot rush of shame. She sat up, deleted the game before she could argue with herself, and set a timer for forty minutes. The first question took her twenty. But she did it.

qa.q: Where did Zainab work before her free hour?
qa.a: She closed up her father's tailoring shop in Bhopal.

qa.q: Why did the farming game keep winning over the olympiad papers?
qa.a: Zainab felt tired after the shop, and the game's instant chimes felt rewarding right now while April felt like another planet.

qa.q: Which of Zainab's steps is most likely to help, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the game before arguing with herself and setting a forty-minute timer, because it removes the instant reward and makes the study hour concrete.

qa.q: What would change if Himani hadn't messaged?
qa.a: Zainab might have kept putting off the papers until April, without a nudge that made the goal feel close and real.

passage: The half-yearly exams were in three months, and Nitin had a plan: two hours of maths every evening. On Monday at seven, he sat at his desk in their Hyderabad flat. Then his phone buzzed. Kamal: "New season live. One match?" One hour of gaming felt bright and real, right now. A good grade in three months felt like a fog. "Just one match," Nitin typed. One became three. At ten he closed the laptop, guilty. "Tomorrow, two hours for sure." On Tuesday, the same thing. By Friday, the maths book hadn't moved. His mother noticed the unopened book and asked, "What if you play after maths, not before?" Nitin grumbled, but tried it on Saturday. Maths first felt awful for twenty minutes. Then the game felt like a reward, not a thief.

passage: Last year, in Class 10, I lost a whole term to one habit. I'm Leela, and every evening I'd tell myself: one hour of the mobile game, then study. The game was right there, glowing, full of little rewards. The board exams were in March. March felt like another planet. So the hour became two, then three. In December, my friend Harish showed me his revision chart, half done. I hadn't started. That night I cried, and my mother didn't scold me. She just asked, "What does March-Leela want from tonight-Leela?" I thought about it for a long time. March-Leela wanted a chance. So we made a deal: forty-five minutes of study first, then the game, and my phone slept in the kitchen after ten. It felt terrible the first week. By February it felt normal.

qa.q: Where did Leela's phone sleep after ten?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling in December when Harish showed his chart?
qa.a: Leela felt panicked and ashamed, crying that night because nothing had been started while Harish was half done.

qa.q: What deal did Leela make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Forty-five minutes of study before the game and the phone in the kitchen after ten, which made the future goal count tonight.

qa.a: Harish probably didn't expect to upset Leela and may have felt worried when he realised she hadn't started.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 11. Written by Aditi.
Parveen came to see me after failing the physics unit test. She was honest: every evening she plans to study at seven, then plays "one match" of an online game, which turns into three hours. "The exam is two months away," she said. "The game is right now. It feels so much better." She knows the board exam matters. It just doesn't feel real on a Tuesday night.
I didn't lecture. I asked what would make the exam feel closer. She suggested putting her target marks on a sticky note on her monitor.
What I did next: we agreed on a small deal. Forty minutes of physics first, then one match as a reward, with a timer. We also asked her mother to keep the charger downstairs after ten. We'll review in two weeks.

qa.q: How long does 'one match' usually turn into?
qa.a: It turns into three hours.

qa.q: Why does the game win over studying for Parveen?
qa.a: Parveen feels tempted by the game because it's vivid and fun right now, while the exam two months away feels weak and unreal on a Tuesday night.

qa.q: What deal did Parveen and Aditi agree on, and why might it work?
qa.a: Forty minutes of physics first, then one timed match as a reward, with the charger downstairs after ten, so the fun comes after the work.

qa.q: How might Parveen's mother feel about keeping the charger?
qa.a: Parveen's mother may feel relieved to have a clear role, and hopeful the plan will help without constant arguments.

Wednesday, 1:10 a.m.
I was going to do two chapters of chemistry tonight. Instead I played the new racing game online with Sachin from 9 till now. Every time I thought "last race", Sachin said "one more", and one more felt amazing. The exam is in February. February doesn't feel like anything. The race felt like everything.
The worst bit is that I know. I know chemistry marks go into my board percentage. I know I'll wish I'd studied. But at 11 p.m., future me feels like a stranger I don't care about.

"Just one round," she told herself. One round became the next level, then a team battle with Nilesh from the next lane.
